passage:
Dear Baljeet,
A quick update on the experiment you suggested.
Week one: I gave myself 45 minutes for the conference abstract, set a timer and sent it to you when it rang, typos and all. My hands were actually sweating when I pressed send. You replied with two small suggestions and "Solid start." Nothing terrible happened. I wrote in my notebook: Sent rough. Survived.
Week two: I sent my team lead a half-finished slide deck labelled "rough", 30-minute limit. She fixed one chart and said thanks. Survived again.
Week three: I put a first draft in the team's shared folder before polishing it. Nobody laughed. One person copied my structure.
I'm keeping a list. Eleven rough things sent, zero disasters. The fear is still there, but quieter each time, like a dog that barks less once it knows the postman.
Attached is draft one of my paper. 60 minutes. Tell me what's wrong with it.
Lokesh

qa.q: What time limit did Lokesh set for the conference abstract?
qa.a: 45 minutes.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel pressing send in week one, and how has that changed?
qa.a: Lokesh's hands were sweating with fear, but after eleven rough things and zero disasters, the fear is quieter each time.

qa.q: Why does Lokesh's list of rough things sent help?
qa.a: It records real evidence that nothing terrible happens, slowly retraining the fear through small, controlled exposures.

qa.q: What might Baljeet feel reading this update?
qa.a: Baljeet may be pleased the suggestion worked and glad to be trusted with the rough paper draft.

grounding: Shows a young professional using time limits, rough drafts sent to trusted people and a record of 'nothing terrible happened' to retrain the fear of imperfection.

passage:
Mahima, you asked on the show how I actually got unstuck. Honestly? Tiny experiments.
I'm Deepak, I design app screens, and for two years I didn't share anything until it was pixel-perfect. So my counsellor suggested one rule: set a timer, make something rough, show one trusted person, and write down what happens.
First try, I sketched a login screen on paper in twenty minutes and sent a photo to my old college friend. I nearly threw up. She replied, "Nice flow, button's a bit small." That's it. Nobody fired me. The sky stayed up. I wrote in my notebook: Rough. Shared. Fine.
Second week, I showed a messy prototype in a team meeting. My manager asked a question, I answered, the meeting moved on.
Now I've got a page full of "fine". The fear still shows up, but it's more like background noise. I didn't beat it by thinking. I beat it by collecting evidence.

qa.q: What did Deepak's old college friend reply about the login screen?
qa.a: "Nice flow, button's a bit small."

qa.q: How did Deepak feel sending the first rough sketch?
qa.a: Deepak nearly threw up with fear, after two years of sharing only pixel-perfect work.

qa.q: What made Deepak's experiments work?
qa.a: A timer, a rough piece, one trusted person and writing down what happened built a page of evidence that sharing imperfect work was fine.

qa.q: What might listeners of Mahima's show take from Deepak's story?
qa.a: Listeners stuck on perfect work may feel hopeful that small, safe experiments can quiet the fear without waiting to feel brave.

grounding: Illustrates small timed experiments of sharing rough work with trusted people and noting that nothing bad happened, which gradually eases the fear.

passage:
I share a flat with Dolma, so I've watched her try something new this month. She used to spend three weeks on every grant report before anyone saw it.
This time she set a kitchen timer for ninety minutes. When it rang, she stopped, even though she was frowning. She emailed the rough draft to her old professor with the subject line "Rough, please be honest."
For two days she kept checking her phone. When the reply came, she read it out: "Good bones. Tighten section two." That was it.
She sat back and laughed. "Nothing terrible happened." She stuck a note on the fridge: EXPERIMENT 1: SURVIVED.
I don't know everything she felt. But she seemed lighter. Tenzin, flatmate.

qa.q: How long was Dolma's kitchen timer set for?
qa.a: Ninety minutes.

qa.q: What might Tenzin have noticed about Dolma's feelings over those two days?
qa.a: Dolma seemed anxious, checking her phone often, and then relieved and lighter when the reply came.

qa.q: Which parts of Dolma's experiment help retrain the fear?
qa.a: A time limit, sending a rough draft to a trusted person, and noting that nothing terrible happened.

qa.q: What is it like for Dolma to read "Good bones"?
qa.a: Dolma seems relieved and amused, laughing that nothing terrible happened.

grounding: Shows a flatmate observing a young woman set a time limit, send a rough draft to a trusted person and notice nothing terrible happened.

passage:
Week one: Yamini, who usually rewrote every email five times, set a rule: ten minutes per email, then send. The first one made her heart race. Her colleague Uma replied, "Thanks! Perfect." Nothing bad happened.
Week two: Yamini sent Uma a rough draft of her presentation, labelled "messy version". Uma wrote back two small suggestions. Yamini's hands were shaking as she read it, then she laughed.
Week three: Yamini wrote in her notebook: "Experiments this month: 12. Disasters: 0." She sent her full presentation a day early, without rewriting it a fourth time.

qa.q: How many disasters did Yamini record?
What was Yamini feeling when she sent the first ten-minute email?
qa.a: She felt nervous, her heart racing, before seeing that nothing bad happened.

qa.q: What makes Yamini's experiments helpful over time?
qa.a: Time limits and rough drafts sent to a trusted colleague show again and again that imperfection is safe, retraining the fear.

qa.q: How might Uma see Yamini's messy drafts?
qa.a: Uma seems relaxed and supportive, giving small helpful suggestions without judgement.

grounding: Shows a young woman using time limits and rough drafts sent to a trusted colleague, noting that nothing terrible happened.

passage:
Preeti, beta, you rewrite every email three times? Let me tell you about my first job, at the insurance office.
I was so afraid of mistakes that I'd take an hour on a one-line memo. My boss, old Mr Iyer, called me in. "Nitin, here's an experiment. Write your next report in thirty minutes. Give it to me rough. See what happens."
I was terrified. I wrote it, rough, and handed it over. My hands were sweating. He read it, made two marks with his pen and said, "Good. Send it."
That was all. Nothing collapsed. Nobody laughed.
So I did it again. And again. Each time, the fear got a little smaller. That's how I learned, beta. Small, safe experiments.

qa.q: Who was Nitin's boss at the insurance office?
qa.a: Old Mr Iyer.

qa.q: What was young Nitin feeling when handing over the rough report?
qa.a: Young Nitin felt terrified, hands sweating, afraid the rough work would be judged.

qa.q: In the story, what experiment helped Nitin?
qa.a: Writing a report in thirty minutes and handing it over rough to a trusted boss, then repeating it.

qa.q: What might Mr Iyer have been thinking when he made two marks and said "Good"?
qa.a: Mr Iyer probably wanted to show Nitin calmly that rough work was fine, and felt quietly pleased.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling time-limited rough drafts given to a trusted boss, each one showing nothing terrible happened.

passage: The train to Pune left in forty minutes, and Pradeep had promised himself one thing: the rough proposal would go to Afreen before he boarded. No more polishing. He sat on a plastic chair in the crowded station café, a toddler wailing at the next table and announcements booming overhead, and typed as fast as he could. Section three was thin. The cost table was ugly. At 6:58 his thumb hovered over send, and his heart thudded as if he were stepping off a ledge. He pressed it. Then he boarded and sat by the window, waiting for disaster. At 8:15 Afreen replied: "Good bones. Section three needs one example. Rest is fine." That was it. No disaster. In the small notebook his counsellor had suggested, he wrote: "Sent rough. Nothing terrible happened. Experiment 4."

qa.q: What did Afreen say section three needed?
qa.a: One example.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling as his thumb hovered over send?
qa.a: He was scared, his heart thudding as if stepping off a ledge, because the draft was rough.

qa.q: Why does writing "Nothing terrible happened" in the notebook help?
qa.a: Recording each safe result gives his fear real evidence, slowly retraining it through small controlled experiments.

qa.q: What might Afreen think on receiving a rough draft from Pradeep?
qa.a: Afreen seems to find it perfectly usable, replying calmly with one practical note instead of judgement.

grounding: Shows a person setting a time limit, sending a rough draft to someone trusted and noting that nothing terrible happened, retraining the fear.
